notes.1a: Very few responses gained credit here. The difficulty in measuring the temperature of a solid while heating it was not widely appreciated. Incorrect responses relating to the speed of the reaction and the concurrence of the two reactions were common. A good number doubted that it would be possible to achieve a high enough temperature to decompose KHCO in the laboratory or that the reaction would be incomplete. In fact, the decomposition takes place easily between 100 and 400°C.
notes.1b: (i) The vast majority of candidates followed the instruction in the question to give answers to three decimal places and produced the correct responses. A small number incorrectly answered to two or four decimal places.
notes.1bii: Candidate’s struggled to answer this straightforward question. The uncertainty in the measurement of a mass is estimated as half of the smallest scale division. If a weighing is made using a balance that displays mass to three decimal places, then there is a ± 0.0005 g uncertainty in that measurement. The mass of the sample of solid is calculated as the difference between two mass measurements. Therefore, the absolute uncertainty in the mass of the sample is (2 × ± 0.0005 g) = ± 0.001 g. Working that clearly showed the candidate had used these steps was essential to gain the mark here. Common answers which were not mark worthy included: 0.001×100 0.0005×100 0.005×2×100 =0.04% =0.02% =0.4% 2.503 2.503 2.503
notes.1c: (i) The responses given to this question were either excellent, showing clear understanding of the calculation steps, or rather haphazard, indicating a poor or incomplete grasp. Some common errors in the calculation of q were: • Using (50 + 2.503) g instead of 50 g for mass of the solution. • Using (273 ± 3.5) K in place of 3.5°C as the temperature change. • Units were not required, but had to be correct if given. J mol–1 or kJ mol–1 were commonly incorrectly used. Errors in the calculation of ΔH included: • Failing to give the correct sign (+) for the endothermic process. • Not dividing by the number of moles of KHCO
notes.1cii: Candidates made similar errors here to those made in (c)(i). Common errors in the calculation of q were: • Using (50 + 3.455) g instead of 50 g for mass of the solution. • Using (273 ± 1.5) K in place of 3.5°C as the temperature change. • Units were not required but had to be correct if given. J mol–1 or kJ mol–1 were commonly incorrectly used. Errors in the calculation of ΔH included: • Failing to give the correct sign (–) for the exothermic process. • Not dividing by the number of moles of K CO 2 3
notes.1d: This was generally well answered by candidates assisted by the Hess cycle provided for them in the question. Incorrect responses usually involved a failure to multiply ΔH by two, multiplying ΔH 1 2 by 2 or a confusion of signs (e.g. adding ΔH rather than subtracting it).
notes.1e: Heat loss and/or heat gain was the predominant creditworthy response given. Heat exchange with the surroundings is complicated as the final value is calculated using ΔH values for an endothermic reaction, during which heat energy would be gained from the surroundings, and an exothermic reaction, during which heat energy would be lost to the surroundings. A correct description of heat exchange associated with each reaction was needed if they were specifically mentioned in the response. Few managed to give a sensible second reason for the discrepancy. Impure solid(s) was a popular incorrect response. Vague answers such as ‘inaccurate weighing of the solid’ and ‘the reaction may not have finished’ were common but not creditworthy.
notes.1f: This question asked for a suggested improvement to the apparatus given, not a wholesale replacement of it. The most popular correct responses involved adding a lid to or extra insulation around the polystyrene cup. Some candidates struggled with the distinction between apparatus and reagents, suggesting the use of powdered solids or acid of a different concentration.
notes.1g: The experiment is designed so that the acid is in excess, thus a measuring cylinder might seem the obvious choice to measure the volume of the acid here. However, the experimental procedure states ‘Transfer 50.00 cm3 …’ and the volume of the solution is used in the later calculation of q, so it is important to choose a measurement method capable of achieving this degree of precision and accuracy. Burette was the most popular acceptable response, followed by pipette. The acid being in excess appeared to lead many candidates into thinking a measuring cylinder, the most popular incorrect response, would suffice.
notes.1h: The irritant nature of all three substances means that chemical resistant gloves are required. The explanation of this choice required reference to the hazard information given earlier in the question. A significant number of responses suggested the use of goggles, even though the question began ‘Apart from wearing safety glasses…’.
notes.2a: Diagrams Candidates who have carried out experiments like the one described in the question are at a great advantage when drawing experimental diagrams. The diagrams were not graded in terms of their neatness and a degree of latitude was allowed in their construction. This said, neat and well- presented diagrams are to be encouraged. Most candidates drew a reaction vessel connected to a gas collection device. This set-up would have gained all three marks. The most commonly missing element in the reaction vessel was a device keeping the two reagents (calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid) apart prior to mixing and reaction, for example, by using a divided flask. The reactants had to be shown separate from each other in the flask The addition of hydrochloric acid from a funnel with a tap was not awarded the mark as gas displaced from the reaction vessel by addition of the acid would be collected in the measuring cylinder introducing inaccuracy in measurement. Several candidates included a gas syringe to collect the carbon dioxide even though the question requires collection by displacement of water.
notes.2b: (i) The table of results was completed correct in most cases.
notes.2bii: Selection of suitable scales for the axes caused few problems. There were two obvious scales for the x-axis; the first has one large square equal to 50 s and the other 30 s. The best scale for the y-axis has one large square equal to 10 cm3. The points plotted easily and were generally located accurately on the grid. Drawing a curved line of best fit freehand in an exam requires a good deal of skill and some allowance is made for this. Overall, these lines were drawn well. There were, however, some poor examples and candidates would benefit from plenty of practice in this technique.
notes.2iii: Simply ‘taking more readings’ or ‘repeating the experiment’ does not improve reliability. These extra experimental measurements must be used to obtain a mean or eliminate anomalies to have an effect and gain the mark.
notes.2iv: This proved to be an elusive mark for most candidates who had to recognise that the reason for the anomaly lay in reading volume of carbon dioxide before 240 s. Many candidates had the correct idea but lost the mark because they did not say exactly what was being measured. ‘The recorded volume was too low’ was a common response without any reason being offered. Vague responses such as ‘read too early’ were not credited. Candidates are expected to explain their answers fully and with precision at this level.
notes.2v: Many candidates recognised which lines to construct, and some drew horizontal and vertical lines with great precision. Frequently, the lines were correctly drawn at 46.5 cm3 and 23.25 cm3. A common error was to give the first half life correctly, e.g. 78 s, and then the second half life incorrectly as the sum of the first two, e.g. 160 s instead of 82 s. Calculation of the average was done well.
notes.2vvi: This calculation was successfully executed by most candidates. Credit was given, error carried forward, for the correct use of any calculated value from (b)(v).
notes.2c: Nearly all candidates stated correctly that k would increase, with the majority of these giving half- life decreasing as the correct explanation. Credit was given for explaining in terms of increased rate of reaction. Some candidates gave an extended answer, including unnecessary extra points which sometimes lost the mark. List answers are best avoided.
notes.2d: (i) The candidates completed the first two columns of the table very well. Marks were lost here by: • using a volume of HCl less than 10.0 cm3 as this would not be an excess or • using a volume such as 13.125 cm3 which could not be measured by a standard piece of volumetric glassware, e.g. a burette. Most candidates calculated the concentration of the diluted hydrochloric acid correctly. Common problems included: • Listing the initial concentration of HCl, 2.0moldm–3, rather than the diluted concentration • Being unable to correctly calculate the concentration.
notes.2dii: There was a good understanding of variables shown. ‘Time taken for the fizzing to stop’ was given by almost all candidates. A few incorrectly suggested ‘the volume of distilled water’ or ‘concentration of the acid.’
notes.general_comments:
In general, most responses were well structured and legible. There were few very low marks and the paper
proved to be accessible to all but a very small number. There were very few unattempted (no response)
Some sections of this paper demand knowledge and understanding of experimental methods. It is possible
that a reduction of practical activities owing to the COVID pandemic was a contributing factor in candidate’s
reduced experience of practical activities.
It is most unfortunate when marks are lost for reasons other than lack of chemical knowledge and
understanding. Close reading of the question and heeding the instructions given when forming answers
would avoid such unnecessary losses. Examples in this paper included:
• Using the correct number of significant figures or decimal places in a numerical answer.
• Showing working where requested.
There is also no credit to be gained for rewriting the question as part of the answer.
The command word ‘suggest’ appears often in this paper and is used in two main contexts. It may imply
either that there is no unique answer (e.g. two or more substances may satisfy the given conditions
describing an ‘unknown’), or that candidates are expected to apply their general knowledge to a new
situation. It is important that candidates bear this in mind when answering.
Two areas that appear frequently in this paper and were not widely understood by candidates this series are:
• calculation of percentage error 1(b)(ii)
• and the initial separation of reagents in the reaction vessel when producing a gas whose volume is to be
measured 2(a).
